analysis.one_liner: Caps seniors' yearly Medicare drug costs at $2,000 and makes drugmakers discount brand-name drugs at the counter.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 2019 with only 3 cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild the Medicare Part D drug benefit so that starting in 2022, a senior's annual out-of-pocket drug costs top out at $2,000, with no cost-sharing above that line. To pay for it, brand-name drugmakers would have to hand seniors discounts at the pharmacy counter — 10% off the negotiated price before the cap is reached and 30% off above it — and the government's 80% reinsurance subsidy to drug plans would drop to 20%. The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially the seniors who today face unlimited out-of-pocket drug bills once they fall into catastrophic coverage — the bill eliminates their cost-sharing above the $2,000 cap. Seniors filling expensive brand-name prescriptions would also see lower prices immediately at the pharmacy, because discounts apply at the point of sale rather than years later. Federal taxpayers gain modestly, since the government's reinsurance payments to drug plans fall from 80% to 20% of high-cost claims.

how_it_helps.text: Starting in 2022, the bill sets the Part D annual out-of-pocket threshold at $2,000, increasing each year thereafter, and eliminates beneficiary cost-sharing above that threshold.

Brand-name drug manufacturers must give applicable beneficiaries discounted prices at the point of sale: 90% of the negotiated price before the beneficiary hits the out-of-pocket cap and 70% after, enforced with civil money penalties equal to the missed discount plus 25%.

The bill cuts the federal reinsurance payment to Part D plans from 80% to 20% of high-cost claims after 2021, shifting the financing of catastrophic drug costs onto manufacturer discounts and away from taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the main cost, funding discounts on every brand-name Part D claim above the deductible. Medicare drug plans lose a large federal reinsurance subsidy, though their bids are adjusted to account for the manufacturer discounts. Seniors still pay dispensing fees and costs below their plan's deductible, and beneficiaries whose drugs are generics or off-formulary get no manufacturer discount at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drugmakers and Part D plans

drawbacks.text: Manufacturer discounts apply only to brand-name drugs (FDA-approved under a new drug application or licensed biologic) that are on the patient's plan formulary; seniors whose drugs are generic, off-formulary, or obtained outside the exception process get no discount.

The bill lets a manufacturer terminate its discount agreement for any reason, with the termination taking effect at the end of the current or even the following plan year, which could leave the discount program short-handed in some drug categories.

Because the discounts attach to the 'negotiated price' that plans and intermediaries arrive at — and the bill directs that discount value be factored into plan bids — some of the manufacturers' cost could resurface in Part D premiums rather than fully in lower drug prices.

The Secretary must contract with outside third parties to transmit information and distribute manufacturer funds, adding an administrative layer the Secretary must police for independence and integrity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors, the benefit is real and large: a hard $2,000 annual ceiling on drug costs and discounts at the counter for the brand-name drugs that drive the biggest bills. The financing leans on the party that sets prices — brand-name manufacturers — with the federal government also saving by slashing its reinsurance subsidy. The honest caveats are that discounts only reach brand-name, on-formulary drugs, manufacturers can exit agreements with long lead times, and some cost may migrate into premiums. On balance the design is a serious attempt to cap senior drug costs, and the reason it failed was political, not structural.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two committees and their health subcommittee the day it was introduced, got nothing beyond its sponsor's floor remarks, and died when the Congress ended with no markup and no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 11, 2019, and referred that same day to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, the Committee on Ways and Means.
On October 14, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health of Energy and Commerce, where it stayed.
The last recorded action was the sponsor's introductory remarks on October 30, 2019; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill closed the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 without advancing past subcommittee referral.
Its support was thin from the start: one Democratic sponsor and 3 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers, who never had to fund the point-of-sale discounts or absorb the penalty regime, and the seniors facing catastrophic drug costs, who got no relief. Democratic committee leadership avoided a floor vote on a drug-pricing bill it did not put forward.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows the split; every supporter in the record was a House Democrat (1 sponsor, 3 cosponsors), and it stalled in committees chaired by Democrats in a Democratic-controlled House.

industries.note: They would fund discounts on every brand-name Part D claim — 90% of the negotiated price below the cap, 70% above — with civil penalties for noncompliance, replacing the existing coverage-gap discount program in 2022. Their gain under the status quo was seniors paying far more, so their interest ran against the beneficiaries this bill protects.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and Medicare Advantage drug plans
industries.note: They lose the 80% federal reinsurance subsidy on catastrophic claims, shrinking it to 20%, but their bids are adjusted to reflect the manufacturer discounts and they keep running the benefit. Their revenue structure survives; their risk share rises.

The Secretary must contract with outside third parties to transmit information and distribute manufacturer funds for the new discount program, creating an administrative business whose work serves the discounts seniors receive at the counter.
